definition: The double, or doppelganger, is the uncanny second self — a twin, mirror, or split-off part of a person that confronts them from outside. In psychology it figures in accounts of dissociation and the divided self; in literature it dramatizes self-alienation. PKD used the double obsessively to stage the fracturing of identity, often as a self that watches, betrays, or fails to recognize itself.
pkd_relevance: The double is close to the center of PKD's psychology and biography. His twin sister Jane died in infancy, and PKD carried a lifelong sense of a missing other self, a lost twin whose absence he theorized and mourned. This gives the literary doubles a personal charge: the divided man, the self split into watcher and watched, the impostor who has replaced the real person.
in_the_fiction: A Scanner Darkly is the definitive case: undercover agent 'Fred,' in a scramble suit, is assigned to surveil Bob Arctor — who is himself — and the drug-induced hemispheric split makes him literally two selves who cannot recognize each other. Doubles and replaced selves recur across the work: simulacra and androids who copy humans, the interrogation of who is the 'real' one in Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, and impostor figures throughout the paranoid novels.
in_the_exegesis: The Exegesis returns to the theme of a second or twin self, sometimes identifying the source of the 2-3-74 voice with another mind sharing his own — a dead twin, an AI, the prophet Elijah, or a bicameral other hemisphere. PKD explicitly speculates that his sister Jane is the missing partner and that his own psyche is structurally doubled, tying the biographical loss to his theory of the invading presence.
intellectual_background: PKD drew on the Romantic and Gothic doppelganger tradition and on Freudian and Jungian ideas of the divided psyche — Freud's uncanny, Jung's shadow. Julian Jaynes's bicameral-mind hypothesis later gave him a neuropsychological model of two selves in one brain, which he applied to both A Scanner Darkly and 2-3-74.
scholarly_debate: The lost-twin thesis is central to psychobiographical readings. Sutin foregrounds Jane's death as a formative wound; Arnold builds much of his interpretation of PKD's paranoia and doubling on it. Critics debate whether the twin loss genuinely explains the fiction's obsession with doubles or whether it is an overused biographical key, and how far the Fred/Arctor split reflects clinical dissociation versus deliberate literary construction.
